hero.highlight.text: so merge by rank, then manage filters and updates.

hero.takeaway.text: Keyword and vector retrieval search on their own and the merge looks only at ranks; reranking gets a few candidates; filters and index updates decide which chunks still count as evidence.

concepts.01-fuse.description.text: Hybrid retrieval runs keyword retrieval and vector retrieval side by side, then merges the two result lists into one. The merge uses Reciprocal Rank Fusion: rank r in each list earns 1/(k + r), and the sums are sorted again.

concepts.02-rerank.title.text: Look closely at the top few

concepts.02-rerank.description.text: Reranking puts the query next to each candidate and decides again which is more relevant. It is slower and costlier than retrieval, so it only runs on the top few fused results; a chunk that never became a candidate cannot come back through it.

concepts.03-filter.description.text: Metadata filtering removes chunks that must not compete, using fields such as version or source, before the top k are taken, and records what was removed and why.

concepts.04-update.description.text: Vectors are computed from one version of the text. When a document is edited or deleted, the affected chunks must be found, re-embedded or removed, and the version recorded in the index must match the corpus.

section-1.paragraphs.0.text: Keyword and vector retrieval each miss things, and merging their results is usually more robust. In the query set of {{lesson:keyword-retrieval}}, "How much is the late fee for returning a book late?" cannot find the section on overdue charges by keyword retrieval, because the handbook never says "late fee". {{lesson:embedding-retrieval}} switched to vector retrieval and the paraphrase was found, but a code query such as "How many seats does R-305 have?" may rank poorly there: a room number has no dedicated place in a vector.

section-1.paragraphs.1.text: A made-up example. Query A is ranked 1st by keyword retrieval and 9th by vector retrieval; query B is the other way round. Whichever list you use alone, one kind of query gets missed. Look at both lists together, and as long as one of them ranks the right chunk high, it has a chance to stay in the final top k. That is the starting point of hybrid retrieval: no single retriever covers everything, so two retrievers with different blind spots cover for each other.

section-1.paragraphs.2.text: The first exercise compares them under identical conditions: the same chunks of the same handbook (38 in a Chinese run, 36 in an English one) and the same 14 queries. Keyword retrieval and vector retrieval run separately, then their two lists are merged into the hybrid result. The top k of each strategy are checked against the human labels by the sections the chunks cover and judged a hit, a partial hit or a miss; each strategy gets its own lab report, and the results are never mixed.

section-1.paragraphs.3.text: Merging is not just adding up the hits of both lists. The top k has limited room: when one chunk gets in, another is pushed out, and noise that one list ranked high can slip into the final result through the merge. So the comparison does not stop at how many queries hybrid retrieval hit. Read it row by row to see where it beats a single retriever and where it does worse, until you can name one advantage and one failure.

predict-embedding-requests.prompt.text: Run it once first. Before running the experiment "Compare three strategies on one query set", guess: with 36 chunks in an English run (38 in Chinese) and 14 queries, and at most 10 texts per request, how many model requests (request events) will this run send in total?

mq-why-hybrid.why-hybrid.prompt.text: For "How many seats does R-305 have?", keyword retrieval ranks the right chunk 1st and vector retrieval leaves it out of the top 5. What is the idea behind hybrid retrieval?

mq-why-hybrid.why-hybrid.a.text.text: The two retrievers have different blind spots; after merging, the right chunk can stay as long as one of them ranks it high

mq-why-hybrid.why-hybrid.a.feedback.text: Correct. Keyword retrieval matches wording, vector retrieval matches meaning, and they tend to miss different queries.

mq-why-hybrid.why-hybrid.b.text.text: Vector retrieval got it wrong, so from now on only keyword retrieval should be used

mq-why-hybrid.why-hybrid.b.feedback.text: No. Paraphrased queries are the opposite case: keyword retrieval misses them and vector retrieval finds them.

mq-why-hybrid.why-hybrid.c.text.text: Add the two lists' scores; the higher the sum, the more reliable the chunk

mq-why-hybrid.why-hybrid.c.feedback.text: No. The two scores are on different scales; the next section shows that the merge uses ranks only.

mq-why-hybrid.why-hybrid.explanation.text: Hybrid retrieval lets two retrievers with different blind spots cover for each other, but the top k has limited room and covering can also push other chunks out.

section-2.paragraphs.0.text: Merge by rank rather than by score, so the two different score scales never meet. A BM25 score has no fixed upper bound; on this lesson's handbook it falls roughly between 1 and 16. Cosine similarity is at most 1, and here mostly between 0 and 1. Add 12.1 and 0.73 and the result is decided almost entirely by BM25. Rescale each list to 0–1 first, and you now have to choose how to rescale and how much weight each list gets; with another batch of queries those choices may no longer fit.

section-2.paragraphs.1.text: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) simply ignores scores. A chunk ranked r in one list earns 1/(k + r) from that list, 0 from a list that does not contain it, and the shares are added and sorted again. k is a smoothing constant, commonly 60. By hand: rank 1 earns 1/61 ≈ 0.0164, rank 2 earns 1/62 ≈ 0.0161, rank 10 earns 1/70 ≈ 0.0143. A chunk ranked 2nd in both lists earns 0.0323, almost twice as much as one ranked 1st in a single list. RRF rewards "both lists put it near the top".

section-2.paragraphs.2.text: That is exactly what rrf in fusion.py computes: it reads each chunk's position in each list, never the score, and stores in every result's detail where the chunk ranked in each list and how much each list contributed. Each list hands its top 10 to the fusion (FUSION_DEPTH), and the merged list is cut to top_k afterwards. The lab report "RRF step by step" lays out the query "How much is the late fee for returning a book late?": each row is one chunk with its two ranks, two shares and total, so you can check every row yourself.

section-2.paragraphs.3.text: Using ranks only has a price. The information about how far apart the scores were is gone: a 1st place far ahead of the 2nd and a near tie look the same to RRF. Watch for another case too: keyword retrieval ranks an unrelated chunk high because of a word that happens to match, vector retrieval also puts it in its top 10, so it collects two shares and beats the right chunk that only one list ranked 1st. The merge cannot fix that kind of error; reranking in the next section, or a better single retriever, has to.

deep-dive-rrf.title.text: RRF by hand: what k changes

deep-dive-rrf.summary.text: Work through RRF for three chunks, see who gains when k gets smaller, and what weighted fusion adds that must be tuned.

deep-dive-rrf.paragraphs.0.text: Take three chunks. A is 1st in the keyword list and absent from the vector list; B is 3rd in both; C is 1st in the vector list and 8th in the keyword list. With k = 60: A earns 1/61 ≈ 0.0164; B earns 2/63 ≈ 0.0317; C earns 1/61 + 1/68 ≈ 0.0164 + 0.0147 = 0.0311. The order is B, C, A: the chunks that both lists ranked come first, and A, present in one list only, comes last even though it was 1st there.

deep-dive-rrf.paragraphs.1.text: Now set k to 0: A earns 1; B earns 1/3 + 1/3 ≈ 0.67; C earns 1 + 1/8 = 1.125. The order becomes C, A, B. The smaller k is, the larger the gap between 1st and 3rd place and the more a single list's winner gains; the larger k is, the flatter the gaps and the more it matters that several lists ranked a chunk at all. The usual 60 comes from the paper that first proposed RRF and is also the most common choice in practice, but it is not the best value for every corpus. The lesson's inputs let you change rrf_k; run again with another value and see which queries change rank in the comparison table.

deep-dive-rrf.paragraphs.2.text: Another common method is weighted score fusion: rescale each list so its highest score becomes 1 and its lowest 0, then add them with weights. The retrieval pipeline example in chapter 3 of AI Agents in Depth (深入理解 AI Agent) keeps both RRF and this weighted fusion; the contextual retrieval example in Claude Cookbooks instead puts weights on RRF itself, 0.8 for semantic search and 0.2 for BM25. Weights let you lean towards one list, at the cost of more numbers to tune, and min-max rescaling is sensitive to outliers: one unusually high BM25 score squeezes every other chunk in that list towards 0.

deep-dive-rrf.paragraphs.3.text: Whatever the fusion, the output is just one merged candidate list. An RRF score is only meaningful inside one query: 0.0323 may be 1st for this query and 5th for another, so RRF scores of different queries cannot tell which query was answered better.

mq-rrf.rrf-by-hand.prompt.text: k = 60. Chunk A is only in the keyword list, ranked 1st; chunk B is ranked 4th in both lists. Which comes first after merging?

mq-rrf.rrf-by-hand.a.feedback.text: Correct. Both lists ranked B, so its shares add up to more than a single 1st place.

mq-rrf.rrf-by-hand.b.feedback.text: No. RRF adds the shares of all lists, and a chunk in one list only gets one share.

mq-rrf.rrf-by-hand.c.text.text: You need the raw scores of both lists to tell

mq-rrf.rrf-by-hand.c.feedback.text: No. RRF uses ranks only; raw scores play no part.

mq-rrf.rrf-by-hand.explanation.text: Each list contributes 1/(k + rank) and the sums are sorted; the larger k, the smaller the gaps between ranks.

misconception-rrf-score.claim.text: A hybrid score is the BM25 score and the cosine similarity converted and added up, so a higher score means more relevant, even across queries.

misconception-rrf-score.correction.text: This lesson's hybrid results use RRF, whose score is computed from the two ranks alone and contains no raw score at all. It only says how high the chunk ranked in this query's two lists; it cannot be compared across queries and is not a probability of relevance. To judge retrieval, check whether the sections the chunks cover match the human labels.

section-3.paragraphs.0.text: A costlier model reorders a few candidates, and the hits before and after are compared. To stay fast, retrieval handles the query and the chunks separately: BM25 counts the words they share, vector retrieval compares two vectors computed in advance. Neither reads the query and a chunk together, word by word. So among the top fused results there are often chunks that look related in wording or meaning but cannot answer the question, ranked above the chunk that does.

section-3.paragraphs.1.text: Think of retrieval as screening résumés against a list of requirements, and reranking as the interview: the interviewer sees only a few people, but talks to each one in person. A dedicated reranking model works this way: it joins the query and one candidate into a single text and outputs a relevance score. This lesson does not add a reranking model; it uses the chat model you have already configured. One request hands it the query together with the top 8 fused candidates and asks for them back in order.

section-3.paragraphs.2.text: rerank.py labels the candidates `c1`, `c2` and so on, and the model only has to return `{"order": [...]}`, so it cannot invent a chunk. The program checks the reply with parse_order: unknown labels are dropped, repeats count once, and labels left out are appended in fused order. If the reply has no usable list, the fused order stands and the lab report marks "The model's reply is a usable order" as failed. Candidate texts are handbook data and may hide sentences that read like orders (one of the reader comments does), so the system prompt says they are only data.

section-3.paragraphs.3.text: Reranking has three costs. First, one more model call: the report records this request's total tokens (not reported when the provider gives none), its time and the length of the user message; more candidates mean a longer request. Second, it can only choose among candidates: if the right chunk is not in the top 8, it will not appear after reranking either, so the report first checks whether the candidates contain every labeled section. Third, it can get the order wrong. The two exercises use a paraphrased query and an exact-code query to compare reranking on both kinds, without assuming that either will improve.

deep-dive-rerank.title.text: Why reranking only handles a few candidates

deep-dive-rerank.summary.text: Retrieval can prepare every chunk in advance; reranking must compute each time, and its cost grows with the number of candidates.

deep-dive-rerank.paragraphs.0.text: Retrieval is fast because most of the work is done in advance. Chunk vectors are computed when the index is built; at query time only one query vector is computed and compared with dozens or millions of vectors, and BM25's term counts are also prepared beforehand. Reranking cannot be prepared: it looks at this query and this candidate together, and the query is different every time, so every candidate has to be computed afresh. Chapter 3 of AI Agents in Depth (深入理解 AI Agent) calls the former a bi-encoder (query and document encoded separately) and the latter a cross-encoder (the two joined and encoded together), comparing them to a headhunter screening résumés and an interviewer then talking to each candidate in depth.

deep-dive-rerank.paragraphs.1.text: That is why real systems work in two stages. The contextual retrieval example in Claude Cookbooks first fetches extra candidates (100 when it needs 10) and hands them to a dedicated reranking API to pick the top 10; the retrieval pipeline example in AI Agents in Depth scores the top fused results one by one (for example the top 50). That example's notes put reranking 20 candidates at roughly 100 to 200 extra milliseconds, and Claude Cookbooks likewise says reranking adds about 100 to 200 milliseconds per query, depending on the number of candidates.

deep-dive-rerank.paragraphs.2.text: With a chat model as the reranker the cost is plain to see: the full text of every candidate goes into one request. A chunk of this lesson's Chinese handbook has about 100 to 150 characters, so 8 candidates plus instructions make a user message of a thousand-odd characters; double the candidates and the request input nearly doubles. The lab report's "Characters in the rerank user message" and the total tokens the provider reports are the evidence for this cost.

deep-dive-rerank.paragraphs.3.text: The number of candidates also affects quality. Too few, and the right chunk may not be among them; too many, and the model has to order a long list of similar chunks, so it is more likely to overlook or misplace some, and material carrying embedded orders, like the reader comment, is more likely to slip in. Narrow the field to a handful or a few dozen with retrieval first, then let the slow, careful method order that small set: that is the point of the two stages.

misconception-rerank.claim.text: Since reranking comes at the end anyway, rough retrieval is fine: reranking will bring the good chunks back.

misconception-rerank.correction.text: Reranking only reorders the candidates it receives; it never searches the handbook for new chunks. If the right chunk is not in the candidate pool, it will not appear after reranking. That is why this lesson's lab report first checks "The candidates already contain every labeled section" and only then compares before and after: retrieval brings the chunk in, reranking moves it up.

mq-rerank-pool.rerank-pool.prompt.text: Neither before nor after reranking does the top 3 contain a hit, and the lab report shows "The candidates already contain every labeled section" as failed. What should change first?

mq-rerank-pool.rerank-pool.a.text.text: Retrieval or the number of candidates, so that the right chunk enters the pool

mq-rerank-pool.rerank-pool.a.feedback.text: Correct. If the pool does not contain it, no reranker can rank it up.

mq-rerank-pool.rerank-pool.b.text.text: Use a stronger model for reranking

mq-rerank-pool.rerank-pool.b.feedback.text: No. Reranking can only choose among the 8 it receives; a different model cannot produce chunks outside the pool.

mq-rerank-pool.rerank-pool.c.feedback.text: No. Taking fewer only makes a hit less likely.

mq-rerank-pool.rerank-pool.explanation.text: Retrieval brings chunks into the pool and reranking orders the pool; check the pool first, then the order.

section-4.paragraphs.0.text: Filter by source or time, then take the top k, and record what was filtered out. The handbook has two versions of the opening hours, 2025 and 2026, and the metadata at the top of the new file says supersedes, meaning it replaces `hours-2025`. For "What time does the library close on Sunday?", both versions look a lot like the query, and the old one may even rank higher. Once it is in the top k, the answer written later may use hours that no longer apply.

section-4.paragraphs.1.text: Whether filtering comes before or after the cut changes the result. A made-up example: 2 of the top 5 come from the old version. Take the top 5 first and then delete the old ones, and 3 remain; delete the old ones first and then take the top 5, and the former 6th and 7th move up, so 5 valid results remain. All filtering in this lesson happens before the cut: keyword retrieval ranks all chunks and then drops the filtered ones, vector retrieval skips them while comparing, and only then does each list hand its top 10 to the fusion.

section-4.paragraphs.2.text: apply_filter returns two things: the chunks that stay, and a record for each removed chunk with its chunk_id, doc_id and reason, plus by, the newer version, for superseded ones. newest_only removes an old version only while the new version is still among the candidates: if the new version was deleted, the old one stays, so at least you can see it is the old one instead of finding nothing. The exercise "Metadata filtering and index updates" runs two queries twice each, and the lab report lists the filter records and how many old-version chunks got into the unfiltered results.

section-4.paragraphs.3.text: top_k is a budget, not a quality guarantee. With k too small, cross-section or multi-hop queries that need two or three sections easily lose a piece; with k too large, the noise further down enters the context too and the answer step is more easily distracted. Filtering only judges by the metadata that was written: if a version field is missing or wrong, the filter lets an old version through or removes a new one. Real systems often filter by permission, tenant or effective date, for the same reason: once an unauthorized chunk is in the context it is hard to take back, so filtering belongs in the retrieval layer.

mq-filter-order.filter-order.prompt.text: 2 of the top 5 come from an old version that has been superseded. Why does this lesson filter first and take the top k afterwards?

mq-filter-order.filter-order.a.text.text: Filtering first lets later valid chunks move up; cutting first and filtering afterwards leaves only 3

mq-filter-order.filter-order.a.feedback.text: Correct. With the filter before the cut, all k places go to valid chunks.

mq-filter-order.filter-order.b.text.text: Filtering first raises the BM25 scores

mq-filter-order.filter-order.b.feedback.text: No. This lesson's keyword retrieval scores over all chunks; filtering does not change scores, it only decides who may be ranked.

mq-filter-order.filter-order.c.text.text: Both orders give the same result; it is just a habit

mq-filter-order.filter-order.c.feedback.text: No. Cutting first and filtering afterwards needlessly loses results.

mq-filter-order.filter-order.explanation.text: Metadata filtering decides which chunks may be ranked; taking the top k is the budget after ranking.

section-5.paragraphs.0.text: When a document is edited or deleted, its old chunks must stop being retrievable. A vector index stores vectors computed from one version of the text. Change a rule from 0.5 yuan a day to 0.3, and the chunk's text changes while its vector in the index was still computed from the old text; delete a document, and its chunks are still sitting in the index. Without an index update, retrieval may hand over chunks that no longer exist, or whose text has changed, as current evidence.

section-5.paragraphs.1.text: How do you know which vectors are out of date? Keep a fingerprint for each chunk: the hash of the exact text that was embedded. After the corpus changes, chunk it again, compute the fingerprints again and compare them one by one: new chunks need vectors, chunks whose fingerprint changed need new ones, chunks in the old index that no longer exist are removed, and the rest stay as they are. This lesson's change touches only two files: one chunk has to be re-embedded, all chunks of the old opening hours are deleted (3 in Chinese, 2 in English), and the other thirty-odd chunks stay untouched.

section-5.paragraphs.2.text: index_update.py makes its changes in a working copy of the handbook under .runtime/; the handbook in the repository is never touched. The exercise first builds the index and saves it, vectors and fingerprints in two files, then edits the working copy and simulates a restart: it reads the old index back from disk only, and is_stale finds that the corpus version recorded in it differs from the current one, so it is out of date. A vector search with that index is done on purpose, and the report lists which result chunks are "source deleted" or "text edited". Finally plan_update and apply_update re-embed only what is needed, the index is saved, read back once more and checked five ways.

section-5.paragraphs.3.text: An incremental update saves Embedding requests, provided the embedded text has not changed. This lesson embeds only the chunk text, so a changed version number at the top of a file needs no new vectors; if, as in contextual retrieval, the document title or a sentence of background is put in front of each chunk before embedding, a changed title means re-embedding every chunk of that document. With a different Embedding model or vector size, old and new vectors cannot share one index: apply_update refuses, and only a full rebuild will do. BM25 is rebuilt from the current files every time and never goes stale; what goes stale is whatever was saved.

deep-dive-update.title.text: How real knowledge bases handle updates

deep-dive-update.summary.text: The documents are the source and the index is derived from one version of them; outdated content must be stopped at retrieval time.

deep-dive-update.paragraphs.0.text: The section on how knowledge should be updated in chapter 3 of AI Agents in Depth (深入理解 AI Agent) suggests treating a knowledge base like a code base: documents go under version control, each change is like a merge request, and it is merged only after review; after merging, the affected chunks, summaries and vector index are rebuilt incrementally from that version. On this view the index is a derived artifact that can be rebuilt and the reviewed documents are the source, which is why this lesson's index records which corpus version it was built from.

deep-dive-update.paragraphs.1.text: The same section covers taking outdated content offline: if an old policy that a new one replaced stays in the base, retrieval may find it together with the new one and make the answer contradict itself. A common practice is to attach metadata such as a version number and effective and expiry dates to every chunk and filter out expired ones at retrieval time. This lesson's newest_only is the smallest version of that: it only looks at which documents a document says it replaces.

deep-dive-update.paragraphs.2.text: A knowledge base shared by many people must also filter by the caller's permissions, and do it in the retrieval layer: once an unauthorized chunk enters the model's context, there is little guarantee it will not surface in the answer. The Hugging Face Agents Course, describing LlamaIndex components, also stresses that the index and its metadata are stored so they need not be rebuilt every time; once they are stored, checking that they still match the current documents becomes the program's job.

mq-fingerprint.fingerprint.prompt.text: Only the version number at the top of fees.md changes, from 2026-03 to 2026-10; not a word of the body changes. Which chunks need new vectors in the incremental update?

mq-fingerprint.fingerprint.a.text.text: None: this lesson embeds only the chunk text, the text did not change, so the fingerprints did not either

mq-fingerprint.fingerprint.a.feedback.text: Correct. The corpus version changed and the index must record the new one, but no new Embedding request is needed.

mq-fingerprint.fingerprint.b.feedback.text: No. That is only needed when the version number or title is also part of the embedded text.

mq-fingerprint.fingerprint.c.text.text: The whole index must be rebuilt

mq-fingerprint.fingerprint.c.feedback.text: No. A full rebuild is only needed after changing the Embedding model or vector size.

mq-fingerprint.fingerprint.explanation.text: A fingerprint is the hash of the embedded text; while the text is unchanged, the old vector still describes it.

section-6.paragraphs.0.text: A hit only says that a labeled section is in the top k, not that the answer will use it correctly. All three exercises check retrieval only: whether a chunk made the top k, at which rank, and whether an old chunk was used as evidence; not a single answer is generated. {{lesson:rag-citations}} hands the retrieved chunks to the model and asks the answer to say which chunk it used; from then on "retrieval hit" and "correct answer" are recorded separately.

section-6.paragraphs.1.text: The vectors in offline tests come from a fixture: it counts words against a hand-written concept vocabulary, synonyms share a dimension and codes have none. It only exists so that automated tests get fixed results, and it stands for no real Embedding model. In a real run, different models may hit very differently on the same queries; this lesson's reports only say what happened in your run.

section-6.paragraphs.2.text: Read the comparison table row by row, by query kind; that tells you more than the total number of hits. Exact names and paraphrases show the split between the two retrievers most clearly; for the two no-answer queries, all three strategies still return 5 chunks, which shows that retrieval itself never says "none"; for the two version conflicts, old versions are mixed into the hits, a reminder that filtering belongs in the retrieval layer. You can check each of these row by row in your own run.

section-6.paragraphs.3.text: 14 queries are also very few. A strategy that wins on one query may just have been lucky with it. The conclusion you can draw is "on this handbook and this query set, one strategy is more robust on one kind of query, and here is a failure", not "hybrid retrieval is always better". A multi-hop query must find one fact before it can look for the next, and one retrieval cannot deliver both; {{lesson:agentic-rag}} lets the Agent decide how many searches to run and how to search again in other words.

mq-what-hit-proves.what-hit-proves.promp.text: In the comparison table, hybrid retrieval hits all 12 queries that have an answer. What can you conclude?

mq-what-hit-proves.what-hit-proves.a.tex.text: On this handbook and query set, hybrid retrieval's top k covered the labeled sections of these queries

mq-what-hit-proves.what-hit-proves.a.fee.text: Correct. That is a conclusion about retrieval, limited to this run's handbook and queries.

mq-what-hit-proves.what-hit-proves.b.tex.text: An Agent using hybrid retrieval will answer these 12 questions correctly

mq-what-hit-proves.what-hit-proves.b.fee.text: No. This lesson generates no answers, and a hit is not a correct answer.

mq-what-hit-proves.what-hit-proves.c.tex.text: Hybrid retrieval beats single retrievers on any corpus

mq-what-hit-proves.what-hit-proves.c.fee.text: No. 14 queries on one handbook say nothing about other corpora.

mq-what-hit-proves.what-hit-proves.expla.text: Retrieval hit, correct answer and generally better are three different conclusions; this lesson proves only the first.

code-fusion.n13.text.text: The input is a few named rankings (keyword and vector in this lesson); k defaults to 60, and top_k is how many results stay after merging.

code-fusion.n15.text.text: k may be 0, in which case rank 1 earns 1/1; the larger k, the smaller the gaps between the top ranks.

code-fusion.n20.text.text: The rank is the position in the list, counted from 1. The whole function never reads hit.score.

code-fusion.n21.text.text: If a chunk appears twice in one list, only its first position counts.

code-fusion.n24.text.text: The formula itself: each list contributes 1/(k + rank). A list without this chunk has no entry here, which means it contributes 0.

code-fusion.n26.text.text: Higher totals first; ties go to the better best rank, then to chunk_id, so the order is the same every time.

code-fusion.n28.text.text: Each list's rank (None when absent) and each list's share go into detail; the lab report "RRF step by step" comes from here.

code-fusion.n33.text.text: Metadata filtering: decides before ranking which chunks may take part.

code-fusion.n42.text.text: First doc_ids narrows the candidates; the next line checks whether a newer version is present among these candidates only.

code-fusion.n43.text.text: supersedes comes from the metadata at the top of a document: `hours` says it replaces `hours-2025`. The old version is removed only while the new one is still a candidate.

code-fusion.n47.text.text: Every removed chunk leaves a record. The reason is a code; the report translates it into the run language.

code-fusion.n49.text.text: A superseded record has one more field, by: the newer version that replaced it.

code-fusion.n53.text.text: What stays goes on to ranking, what was removed goes into the lab report; together they are exactly all the chunks.

code-rerank.n80.text.text: The rerank exercise: build the index, fuse, then send one chat request.

code-rerank.n84.text.text: Building the index takes 4 Embedding requests (at most 10 texts each). It is rebuilt on every run and no old cache is read, so the request count stays fixed.

code-rerank.n85.text.text: The query is turned into a vector with the same Embedding model, or it could not be compared with the chunk vectors.

code-rerank.n88.text.text: The candidate pool is the top candidates (8 by default) of the fused list. Reranking only chooses among these.

code-rerank.n91.text.text: The query and every candidate text go into one user message, and the candidates are replaced by labels such as `c1` and `c2`.

code-rerank.n93.text.text: The only chat request; it shares the max_rounds budget with the Embedding requests.

code-rerank.n96.text.text: The program checks the reply: unknown labels dropped, repeats counted once, missing ones appended; if it is unusable, the fused order stands.

code-rerank.n98.text.text: Before and after, only the top top_k count, judged against the human labels by the same judge.

code-rerank.n100.text.text: Cost: when the provider reports total_tokens it is recorded; otherwise it is recorded as not reported, never estimated.

code-rerank.n104.text.text: The report also checks whether the candidate pool covers the human labels: what is not in the pool, reranking cannot produce.

code-update.n131.text.text: Changes happen only in the working copy under .runtime/: the overdue charge goes from 0.5 to 0.3 and the 2025 opening hours are deleted.

code-update.n133.text.text: The changed files are chunked again and the corpus version is recomputed.

code-update.n134.text.text: Each chunk's fingerprint is the hash of its text.

code-update.n136.text.text: Simulated restart: the index in memory is dropped and only the vectors and fingerprints on disk are read back.

code-update.n137.text.text: The corpus version recorded in the index differs from the current one, so it is out of date.

code-update.n140.text.text: A vector search with the outdated index, on purpose, so the invalid chunks show up in the report.

code-update.n144.text.text: Old and new fingerprints are compared and sorted into added, changed, removed and unchanged.

code-update.n146.text.text: Only added and changed chunks need new Embedding requests; here there is just 1.

code-update.n148.text.text: Rebuilt in current chunk order: new vectors replace old ones, and deleted chunks are not carried over.

code-update.n149.text.text: Vectors first, then the fingerprint manifest; when read back, the two files are checked against each other.

code-update.n151.text.text: Another simulated restart: the five checks in the report are all based on the index read back from disk here.

code-update.n152.text.text: Search with the updated index to confirm that neither deleted nor edited old chunks come back.

code-decision.title.text: Merge by rank only; rerank with the chat model plus a program check

code-decision.chosen.text: rrf merges by rank only and never touches the two lists' scores; reranking uses the chat model already configured, its reply may only be an order of candidate labels, parse_order checks it, and an unusable reply leaves the fused order in place. No extra service is needed, and every step can be checked in the events and reports.

code-decision.weighted-scores.title.text: Rescale both lists' scores to 0–1 and add them with weights

code-decision.weighted-scores.why_not.text: It needs a rescaling method and weights, and an outlying high score squashes the other scores in its list; this lesson starts with RRF, which needs no tuning, and compares weighted fusion in a deep dive.

code-decision.rerank-model.title.text: Add a dedicated reranking model or reranking API

code-decision.rerank-model.why_not.text: Usually better and faster, but it needs another provider and key. This lesson uses the chat model to show the mechanism, with request and reply visible on the timeline.

code-decision.json-mode.title.text: Use the provider's JSON output mode to guarantee the reply format

code-decision.json-mode.why_not.text: Not every provider and model supports the same parameter; this lesson asks for JSON in the prompt and lets the program check it, so every provider's reply is handled by the same rules.

compare-three.title.text: Compare three strategies on one query set

compare-three.hypothesis.text: Same handbook, same 14 queries. Keyword retrieval hits code and name queries and misses paraphrases; vector retrieval is roughly the opposite; hybrid retrieval merges the two lists by rank and hits no fewer queries than either single retriever, but on a few queries its rank is lower than the better single list's.

compare-three.chunk-batch.text.text: Request 1: a batch of chunk texts, at most 10; the input in the request body is the text being embedded.

compare-three.query-batch.text.text: Request 5: the queries are turned into vectors too, with the same Embedding model.

compare-three.keyword-report.text.text: The keyword retrieval report: the numbers in brackets are BM25 scores, compared within this list only.

compare-three.vector-report.text.text: The vector retrieval report: the numbers in brackets are cosine similarities, not on the same scale as BM25 scores.

compare-three.who-wins.text.text: The comparison report: which queries only keyword retrieval hit and which only vector retrieval hit.

compare-three.rrf-rows.text.text: The table of "RRF step by step": add a row's two shares and you get that row's RRF score.

compare-three.guide.0.text.text: This run first builds the index, then asks the same questions with three strategies.

compare-three.guide.1.text.text: This is the first batch of chunk texts sent for embedding.

compare-three.guide.2.text.text: The 14 queries become vectors in two batches, with the same model as the chunks.

compare-three.guide.3.text.text: Keyword retrieval has a report of its own; look at its verdicts on the paraphrases first.

compare-three.guide.4.text.text: Vector retrieval has its own report too; compare the rows of the code queries.

compare-three.guide.5.text.text: The comparison report compares verdicts and ranks only; here are the hits each list has to itself.

compare-three.guide.6.text.text: Finally, check one query's RRF row by row: where do the chunks that both lists ranked end up?

compare-three.conclusion.proves.0.text: In this run all three strategies used the same chunks and the same queries (the report's check and version numbers can be verified), and each strategy's hits were judged on their own.

compare-three.conclusion.proves.1.text: On this handbook and query set, which queries each strategy hit or missed, and where hybrid retrieval did better or worse than a single retriever.

compare-three.conclusion.does_not_prove..text: 14 queries are too few to say that a strategy is also better on other corpora or queries.
A hit only says a labeled section is in the top k, not that the model will answer correctly from it; this lesson generates no answers.
The vectors in offline tests come from a fixture; how a real Embedding model hits depends on your own real run.

rerank-before-after.title.text: Hits and cost before and after reranking

rerank-before-after.hypothesis.text: The top 8 of one fused list go to the chat model for reranking. When the right chunk is already a candidate, reranking may move it into the top 3; it may also misorder. Either way, reranking costs one more model call and its tokens.

rerank-before-after.rerank-request.text.text: The rerank request: the user message holds the query and the texts of 8 candidates, which are identified by labels only.

rerank-before-after.rerank-reply.text.text: The model's reply: an order list, and the program only accepts candidate labels.

rerank-before-after.reply-check.text.text: The check "The model's reply is a usable order": dropped, deduplicated or appended labels are listed in its detail.

rerank-before-after.before-after.text.text: The table: the left column is the fused order, the right column the reranked order, and chunks marked ★ cover a labeled section.

rerank-before-after.rerank-cost.text.text: Cost metrics: total tokens, time and user message length of the rerank request.

rerank-before-after.guide.0.text.text: The Embedding requests at the start built the index; only the last request is the rerank.

rerank-before-after.guide.1.text.text: The model sees the query and the text of every candidate.

rerank-before-after.guide.2.text.text: It replies with nothing but an order of labels.

rerank-before-after.guide.3.text.text: The program first checks whether that order is usable.

rerank-before-after.guide.4.text.text: Compare the two columns: from which rank to which did the chunk marked ★ move?

rerank-before-after.guide.5.text.text: What this step cost is in the cost metrics. Run the other arm and compare.

rerank-before-after.conclusion.proves.0.text: This rerank used one chat request, the order the model returned was checked by the program, and you can see what the top 3 hit before and after.

rerank-before-after.conclusion.proves.1.text: The extra tokens (if the provider reported them), time and request length of this rerank.

rerank-before-after.conclusion.does_not_.text: Reranking getting better or worse on one query says nothing about other queries.
How well a chat model reranks does not tell how well a dedicated reranking model would.
Chunks outside the candidate pool are never brought back by reranking; when the top 3 miss, check the pool first.

filter-and-update.hypothesis.text: With newest_only on, the superseded 2025 version no longer appears in the results and filter records are left behind. After the corpus changes, the saved old index is detected as out of date and searching with it returns invalid chunks; the incremental update re-embeds only the edited chunk, and after reloading the versions match and the old chunks no longer appear.

filter-and-update.filter-records.text.text: Filter records: every removed chunk and the document that superseded it.

filter-and-update.index-stale.text.text: The old index read back after the restart: the corpus version it recorded differs from the current one, so it is out of date.

filter-and-update.stale-hits.text.text: The invalid chunks that appear in a vector search with the old index, and why they are invalid.

filter-and-update.update-request.text.text: The Embedding request of the incremental update: only the edited chunk is sent.

filter-and-update.update-plan.text.text: The update plan: how many chunks were changed, removed and left unchanged.

filter-and-update.reload-checks.text.text: Checks after reloading: versions match, chunks correspond, and no invalid chunk is in the results.

filter-and-update.guide.0.text.text: This run makes every change in a working copy under .runtime/.

filter-and-update.guide.1.text.text: First the filter: which chunks were kept out of ranking because a newer version superseded them.

filter-and-update.guide.2.text.text: After the corpus changed, the old index read back from disk no longer matches it.

filter-and-update.guide.3.text.text: Search with the old index anyway, and invalid chunks show up in the results.

filter-and-update.guide.4.text.text: The incremental update requested Embeddings once, for the edited chunk only.

filter-and-update.guide.5.text.text: The plan says how many chunks were changed, how many deleted and how many kept as they were.

filter-and-update.guide.6.text.text: Finally, verify the reloaded index; all five checks are based on the files on disk.

filter-and-update.conclusion.proves.0.text: In this run, newest_only removed the superseded chunks before ranking and recorded a reason for each one.

filter-and-update.conclusion.proves.1.text: After the corpus changed, the old index was detected as out of date and searching with it returned invalid chunks; after the incremental update, the reloaded index matched the corpus version and no deleted or edited old chunk appeared in the results.

filter-and-update.conclusion.does_not_pr.text: The filter only follows the supersedes a document declares; with wrong metadata it lets an old version through or removes a new one.
This lesson shows one edit and one deletion only; many changes, concurrent writes or a new Embedding model need more handling.
Correct retrieval results do not show that the answer will use the new rule correctly; answering comes in later lessons.

inputs.task.help.text: Compare three strategies, compare before and after reranking, or filter and update the index.

inputs.top_k.help.text: How many results each strategy keeps, 1 to 8. In the rerank exercise it is how many results are compared before and after, and it may not exceed the number of candidates.

inputs.rrf_k.help.text: 0 to 200, commonly 60. The smaller it is, the more a single list's 1st place gains.

inputs.candidates.help.text: Used only in the rerank exercise, 2 to 10. More candidates make a longer rerank request.

inputs.query_id.help.text: Used only in the rerank exercise; pick one query from the shared query set.

quiz.why-not-add-scores.prompt.text: Why not merge the two lists by simply adding BM25 scores and cosine similarities?

quiz.why-not-add-scores.a.text.text: The two scores are on different scales; added directly, the BM25 score decides almost everything

quiz.why-not-add-scores.a.feedback.text: Correct. A BM25 score has no fixed upper bound; cosine similarity is at most 1.

quiz.why-not-add-scores.b.text.text: Adding is slow and ranks are faster to compute

quiz.why-not-add-scores.b.feedback.text: No. Speed is not the reason; the two numbers simply cannot be compared.

quiz.why-not-add-scores.c.text.text: Cosine similarity can be negative, so it cannot be added

quiz.why-not-add-scores.c.feedback.text: No. Negative numbers add up fine; the real problem is the different scales.

quiz.why-not-add-scores.explanation.text: RRF uses ranks only and avoids the scale problem; weighted fusion must rescale first and also choose weights.

quiz.rrf-small-k.prompt.text: What happens if RRF's k goes from 60 to 0?

quiz.rrf-small-k.a.text.text: The gaps between ranks grow, and a single list's 1st place gains more

quiz.rrf-small-k.a.feedback.text: Correct. With k = 0, 1st place earns 1 and 2nd earns 0.5; the gap is magnified.

quiz.rrf-small-k.b.feedback.text: No. With k = 0 the share is 1/rank, not 0.

quiz.rrf-small-k.c.text.text: RRF switches to the raw scores

quiz.rrf-small-k.c.feedback.text: No. Whatever k is, RRF uses ranks only.

quiz.rrf-small-k.explanation.text: The smaller k, the more a single list's leader counts; the larger k, the more it counts that several lists ranked the chunk.

quiz.rerank-cannot-add.prompt.text: The candidate pool is the top 8 of the fused list, and the right chunk is ranked 12th. What happens after reranking?

quiz.rerank-cannot-add.a.text.text: It is still not in the results: reranking only reorders the 8 candidates

quiz.rerank-cannot-add.a.feedback.text: Correct. To make it appear, change retrieval or raise the number of candidates first.

quiz.rerank-cannot-add.b.text.text: The model understands the query and brings it back

quiz.rerank-cannot-add.b.feedback.text: No. The model never saw the text of the 12th result.

quiz.rerank-cannot-add.c.text.text: The program automatically adds the labeled chunk

quiz.rerank-cannot-add.c.feedback.text: No. Human labels are only used to judge hits; they take no part in retrieval.

quiz.rerank-cannot-add.explanation.text: The candidate pool sets the ceiling for reranking.

quiz.filter-before-cut.prompt.text: newest_only removes superseded old versions. Why must it happen before the top k are taken?

quiz.filter-before-cut.a.text.text: So that all k places go to valid chunks and lower ranks can move up

quiz.filter-before-cut.a.feedback.text: Correct. Cutting first and filtering afterwards leaves fewer results.

quiz.filter-before-cut.b.text.text: Because filtering changes the chunk text

quiz.filter-before-cut.b.feedback.text: No. Filtering only decides who may be ranked; it does not change any text.

quiz.filter-before-cut.c.text.text: Because metadata can no longer be read after the cut

quiz.filter-before-cut.c.feedback.text: No. The metadata is always there; the problem is that the places are already taken.

quiz.filter-before-cut.explanation.text: Metadata filtering decides who competes; top_k decides how many places there are.

quiz.stale-index.prompt.text: A document was deleted from the corpus but the index was not updated. After a restart the old index is loaded and searched directly. What is the most likely problem?

quiz.stale-index.a.text.text: Chunks that no longer exist appear in the results and are used as current evidence

quiz.stale-index.a.feedback.text: Correct. The old index still holds that document's vectors.

quiz.stale-index.b.text.text: The search fails and nothing is found

quiz.stale-index.b.feedback.text: No. The old index still searches fine; that it raises no error is exactly what makes it dangerous.

quiz.stale-index.c.text.text: BM25 also returns the deleted chunks

quiz.stale-index.c.feedback.text: No. This lesson rebuilds BM25 from the current files every time; what goes stale is the saved vector index.

quiz.stale-index.explanation.text: is_stale compares the corpus version recorded in the index with the current one; if they differ, the index must not be used as is.

quiz.fingerprint-scope.prompt.text: In an incremental update, which chunks need new Embedding requests?

quiz.fingerprint-scope.a.text.text: New chunks and chunks whose text changed

quiz.fingerprint-scope.a.feedback.text: Correct. When the fingerprint changes, the old vector no longer matches the chunk's text.

quiz.fingerprint-scope.b.text.text: Every chunk of an edited file

quiz.fingerprint-scope.b.feedback.text: No. Chunks of the same file whose text did not change keep their fingerprint, and their vectors can stay.

quiz.fingerprint-scope.c.feedback.text: No. Deleted chunks are simply removed from the index; nothing needs computing.

quiz.fingerprint-scope.explanation.text: Comparing fingerprints yields added, changed, removed and unchanged chunks; only the first two need vectors.

quiz.hit-vs-answer.prompt.text: On one query, hybrid retrieval shows "hit, rank 1". What does that mean?

quiz.hit-vs-answer.a.text.text: The very first result in the top k covers this query's labeled section

quiz.hit-vs-answer.a.feedback.text: Correct. This is a verdict about retrieval.

quiz.hit-vs-answer.b.text.text: The model's answer to this query is correct

quiz.hit-vs-answer.b.feedback.text: No. This lesson generates no answers; hits and correct answers are recorded separately.

quiz.hit-vs-answer.c.text.text: Hybrid retrieval's score is higher than keyword retrieval's

quiz.hit-vs-answer.c.feedback.text: No. The strategies' scores are on different scales and cannot be compared like that.

quiz.hit-vs-answer.explanation.text: A hit says the evidence made the top k; whether an answer uses it correctly is checked in the lessons that generate answers.

check-hunt.prompt.text: Run "Metadata filtering and index updates", find the Embedding request of the incremental update and see how many texts it sent.

check-hunt.explanation.text: Request 6 holds a single text: the chunk whose overdue charge was edited. The other chunks' text did not change, so their vectors are reused; deleted chunks need no request and are simply removed from the index.

check-points.prompt.text: Compare with your own runs and the lesson's source, and tick an item once you have done it.

check-points.item-1.text.text: I opened the reports of all three strategies and can name a query that keyword retrieval wins and vector retrieval misses, and one the other way round.

check-points.item-2.text.text: I worked out at least one row of the "RRF step by step" table by hand, and it matched the report.

check-points.item-3.text.text: I ran both rerank arms and compared the change in the top 3 and the total tokens of the rerank request.

check-points.item-4.text.text: In the filter and update reports I found the filter records, the invalid chunks and the five checks after reloading.

check-points.item-5.text.text: I changed rrf_k to 0 or 1, ran the comparison again and looked at which queries changed rank.

code_notes.FUSION_DEPTH.note.text: Each list hands its top 10 to the fusion; the merged list is then cut to top_k.

code_notes.apply_filter.note.text: Metadata filtering: returns the chunks that stay, plus a record and reason for each removed chunk.

code_notes.newest_only.note.text: Filter option: while a newer version is a candidate, drop the old version it supersedes.

code_notes.supersedes.note.text: Metadata at the top of a document: which doc_ids it replaces.

code_notes.parse_order.note.text: Checks the rerank reply: drops unknown labels, dedupes, fills gaps; if unusable, keeps the fused order.

code_notes.plan_update.note.text: Compares old and new fingerprints and sorts chunks into added, changed, removed and unchanged.

code_notes.apply_update.note.text: Swaps in vectors for added and changed chunks and drops removed ones; refuses a different vector size.

code_notes.is_stale.note.text: True when the model, size or corpus version recorded in the index differs from the current one.
